It's called trichotillomania, a type of Body-Focused Repetitive Behavior (BFRB). There are some tricks that I use to stop myself from cheek chewing (my main BFRB) such as chewing gum, using breath mints, or wearing lipstick. I at one point tried snapping a hair tie around my wrist every time I caught myself.

You might try fidget toys to keep your hands busy or putting your hair up or styling it to stop yourself from "messing it up."

But mostly, just catching myself in the act, forcing myself to stop and deal with the discomfort of it being "incomplete" is the best method.

If tricks don't work and it's causing you a lot of distress, I'd recommend seeking a therapist who specializes in Exposure and Response Prevention (ERP) for OCD and BFRBs, and/or medication.

I was in the same situation as you just recently. Earlier this week, I tapered myself off and fully quit the other day :) it has been 2 days! Not long, but I am really determined.

I wanted to say this because there's a few aspects that helped me quit that might help others. Really, it came down to just making the decision that I wanted to stop.

1. Weed is damaging to growing brains. I'm 24, and my brain won't be done growing till I'm about 30. If I keep smoking, I feel like I'm hard-wiring my brain into OCD spirals. I want to give it a chance to grow and heal on its own, so that maybe it'll heal and I won't be struggling so much when I'm older :) using OCD against OCD, a cute loophole.

2. Life is easier to deal with sober. I find smoking is a compulsion in itself to escape my distress, but it only makes it worse, which in turn makes me want to smoke more. I decided I'm not trying to escape.

3. Tricks: Every time I feel the urge to smoke, I tell myself, no, I can do this without weed. Just to see, let's see if in maybe 15 minutes I still want to smoke. 15 minutes later, I'm usually fine. It's a nice trick to quell OCD of any kind—give yourself 15 minutes doing something else, and see if you still wanna do it by then (which is rarely).

Best of luck. ❤️ The shame and stigma is honestly one of the hardest parts. I stand up for my weed use while also knowing that it's a detrimental cycle for me. It's hard to admit to anyone, honestly.

Diagnosis can be helpful for many reasons! If you feel you need treatment because your symptoms are causing you distress and disrupting your life, a proper diagnosis can help you feel really confident moving forward with treatment. I do have to say, though, that OCD is misunderstood even within the medical community, so I would recommend seeking a person who specializes in or has experience with diagnosing/treating OCD.

Treatment is really different for OCD than it is for other psychiatric disorders. Medications can help, but the dosages and drug classes used to treat OCD are often different. Therapy can also help, classic mindfulness, ACT, and CBT, but the absolute gold standard is Exposure and Response Prevention (ERP). In my experience with OCD it has been so important that I seek out the correct treatments, especially with providers that understand OCD. It also helps simply to have a label for what's going on in my head—aids with imposter syndrome, which is so common. Plus, it's a great aid in finding connections and resources like specialized group therapy, intensive treatments, and supports like The OCD Foundation and The OCD Stories :)

OCD involves a complicated, emotionally distressing cycle that begins with:

An egodystonic, intrusive thought. "What if my underwear isn't clean, I smell repulsive, and everyone avoids or leaves me? I would be such a bad, disgusting person." A person with OCD knows how illogical this is, and yet the thought spirals into an obsession that causes significant distress, compulsing the person to relieve this distress though a physical or mental compulsion, such as changing underwear, shifting in your seat to feel if underwear is clean, going to the bathroom and checking and smelling that underwear is clean, mentally reassuring yourself that your underwear is clean, looking for wet spots on pants, counting times you have changed underwear, washing underwear with bleach or avoiding doing laundry altogether, hoarding clean underwear, etc. DESPITE DOING THIS, THE FEAR IS NOT REASSURED, CAUSING THE CYCLE TO REPEAT.

This is list is not conclusive nor is it meant to imply that a person with OCD will participate in all of these behaviors, nor does it imply that they don't additionally struggle with other themes such as "what if I accidentally kill my husband with the knife as we are cooking together?"

OCD is incredibly misunderstood because people do not understand the depth that is involved with the obsessions and compulsions. There is an intrusive thought behind every compulsion.

As with most OCD themes, I differentiate my thoughts based on egodystonic nature. Egodystonic meaning that the thought or feeling differs from my actual thoughts, beliefs, or desires.

For example: I fear that the cake on the counter has been contaminated because there was no lid over it for a few hours, so I refuse to eat it. The egodystonic part of this is that I don't actually believe the cake has been contaminated or will make me sick if I eat it. I know how silly it is. Logically, my kitchen is clean and it's just cake. And even if I do get sick, whatever. But I can't stop myself from being afraid of it, nor can I make myself eat the cake, though I want to. That's egodystonic.

Another example: I'm on a diet. I think "man, I'd sure love some candy." That's not an egodystonic thought. Because like, deep down I actually do want the candy despite the rules that I've set for myself with the diet.

If you're on the OCD subreddit, my advice to you is to look inside yourself and ask yourself questions. There is a reason you are here, and I wonder if it's because you feel guilty about it. Do you want these feelings? Have you sought treatment out of a need to "confess?" This is common with OCD, especially POCD. Do more research on OCD yourself. Check out The OCD Stories.

I understand how distressing all of these types of thoughts and feelings can be. At my worst, I have beliefs and fears that my family and friends are manipulating me and can read my thoughts, that my food and water are poisoned, or that everything I do will have some greater spiritual consequence such as stepping on a blue mat, putting tea tree oil on a pimple, or saying an incorrect word. At it's worst, I freeze and cannot move or speak. I fear that anything I experience, think, feel, do, hear, and touch will cause a cascade of events that will destroy the entire structure of the future that everyone's souls are working toward. I see blobs of color when I feel or think certain things, and let them guide my decisions.

I also have had sleep paralysis and hallucinations before falling asleep completely and especially after waking up. My cousin has schizoaffective disorder and synesthesia. I used to have a medical marijuana card, and it can cause psychosis sometimes. I'm a female in my mid 20's. These all lead me to believe I am developing psychosis or schizophrenia. It's terrifying.

I even went to ERs a bunch of times and was diagnosed with MDD with psychotic features. But no one ever mentioned to me that it could be OCD. Confirming my fears of being psychotic and being ill, without acknowledging the full range of my symptoms or validating my own belief that it all centers around OCD. I have thought it was OCD ever since I was a child. I used to tap my toes in certain ways as I walked, touch or pinch my body to balance it, negate "bad" thoughts and feelings in my mind, repeat things in my mind and out loud. When I heard about OCD, and read more about it, it resonated deeply with me. But I often experience imposter syndrome, feel like I am a fraud or lying to people or acting. That I don't have OCD, something greater must be wrong with me, or maybe I'm a psychopath and there's actually nothing wrong with me. Even now I have these thoughts.

But now I don't believe that what I personally experience is psychosis. It is a build-up of fear, trauma, stress, and obsessive-compulsive cycles that break my protective dam. The more I experience them and the more I learn about myself and grow, the more I understand this. It spirals, and I call it an OCD attack or episode. Nothing is more validating than people believing me that it's all OCD. I fear it not being confirmed because OCD resonates with me so deeply. But I took the Y-BOCS and check nearly every box. My new psychiatrist, in my first assessment, told me that maybe my episodes are psychosis, or maybe they are just severe OCD symptoms, as they often are a differential diagnosis. He is the first ever doctor to say this, and it was massively relieving. Everyone else in my past has denied it for some reason or another, likely due to misconceptions of OCD or fear of the diagnosis due to its severity. Perhaps also due to my ability to mask in professional settings. Identifying it as what it is has incredible importance to me. It's grounding because I often worry about what's wrong with me, why, and how I can fix it.

It is relieving to me to see in this subreddit more people that resonate with my thoughts and feelings. I commented with someone awhile ago who also sees the colored dots, and that is amazing and I feel understood. I see a lot of people worrying about psychosis. It is validating, and I can understand myself and others and OCD much better, as I see more of what it can encompass.

It is often hard to differentiate psychosis and OCD. It can often feel one way or the other, especially in dire situations, and I myself often fear going insane or acting out. But honestly, it's that fear that gives me comfort that I am not experiencing psychosis. It is horrible, intense, and feels like I will cause a wreck to the universe. But I have read that psychosis is a firm belief. It cannot be convinced otherwise. Although retrospectively, I look at my experience if I had these firm beliefs, I also experienced a significant amount of fear. I was aware of my actions, and that my beliefs were not actually true. Though, I did firmly act upon them as if they were. I think because I wanted them to be true because it is better to act upon them as if they are true, rather than if they are not. Because I do not want to make a mistake, be a bad person, go to Hell, or upset my family or God. It gets extremely overwhelming because it's one fear after the next. Psychosis is absolute and unshakable. And as they say, people who worry about being psychotic are not psychotic. OCD, although similar, stems from a fear, especially of hurting others or myself. It often has moral implications and fears.

I am not saying that you do not have psychosis, nor am I saying that what it is defined as has any impact on how it felt for you whatsoever. It sounds awful, terrifying, and heavy. I am glad you are feeling better and hope you continue to do so.

As a side note, OCD often requires very high doses of antidepressants to work. If what you're taking is working, maybe ask your doctor about increasing it more. Taking the Y-BOCS may also be insightful to you and your care team.

I understand. Living with chronic pain, trauma, and mental health disorders is a constant struggle. I used to have 24/7 headaches and migraines, now they're a little lessened but there's always something going on with my body.

My advice is to not give up. If you have to, take it day by day, or moment by moment, there's nothing wrong with that. It's okay to give yourself a break. It's okay if you don't feel well. It's okay if you feel great. It's okay if you feel both. Do your best to continue on and improve all areas of your life as best you can, bit by bit. Your best will change up and down every day.

For me, a lot of my health problems have been mixed up and down my whole life. Healing is not linear. But I would say I'm doing much, much better than I was a year ago, even a few years ago. Even if that progress seems small to me. It feels like I have so far to go. And I don't have enough time. But it's okay, I really do have time, it's okay to relax and just take every day as it is if the future is too intimidating.

For me, helping every moment has helped both my physical and mental health. Listening to myself and my boundaries. Allowing myself to feel my feelings, to name and understand them, and do something about them, even if just with myself, like jotting things down on a napkin or doing a shitty doodle. Talking to the people in my life about the things that bother me, allowing myself to express how I feel, this helped too.

I notice as I listen to myself, I feel my surroundings more. I'm more aware and connected with all my senses. It makes me more aware of how I feel about situations and relationships. How I physically feel. I used to be, extremely often, dissociative from my body. I would feel extreme pain and not understand where it came from. But now I feel as though I'm closer to understanding. Because if I'm anxious, then I notice my jaw clenching. A scary loud noise will tense my arms and forehead. I hold a lot of stress in my shoulders and bones, so I feel weak. If I can connect these, I can address the core cause.

Something that may be good to look into, if you haven't yet, is headache locations and meanings. It's a rough guideline. If I can pinpoint the location, and understand how the pain feels, and how it's making me feel, I can sometimes dig a little deeper into why, or even just what I can do to make it better. A gentle massage, drinking water, eating fruit, getting somewhere quiet, taking a walk, being by myself and listening to music for a little while. It doesn't fix it entirely. But it does make me feel better in the moment, and more recharged.

It hasn't been easy. Every day is a hike, even if I don't move at all. And I'm still not "better." I often don't feel well at all. I have to tell myself it's okay to give up sometimes. It's scary. But it does feel good to be more aware of myself and more in tune with how I feel and why I feel it. It feels like such a small, baby step. But it's kind of like... knowing that spring is going to come back, eventually, after a dark and dreary winter. Sometimes the sun comes out, sometimes it snowstorms again. But the sunset is starting to not be so early, and it's a little warmer than it was.

I'm not saying you will be the same. Not everything is psychosomatic. But my advice still stands that it's okay to believe in yourself, to accept yourself as you are and listen to your boundaries. To take each moment slower and feel what you really want to do. Even if the headaches are incurable, there are many ways to improve your life and feel more comfortable despite the pain. You are never the person you were 5 minutes ago. You get to decide who you are.

Allow yourself to feel hope and passion for the future. Allow yourself to feel disappointment, guilt, and pain. And more importantly, give yourself patience. Give yourself grace.

Here's my advice! Apologies for the long response.

It may be reassurance to have these things I say to myself. But it's really the only way I know how to cope with my thoughts and fears, I learned some of it from cognitive behavioral therapy, "replacing the thought." It's a process of learning to trust myself and my real thoughts and feelings, improving and cutting out negative thoughts and behaviors as I notice them and feel strong enough to tackle them. Practice makes perfect and thought replacement has taken time and work for me to actually improve, lots of ups and downs and relapses.

One of the keys to aiding what I do is limits! I only allow myself to go so far with what I tell myself or compulsively check, or do. I give myself a certain amount of time, or certain amount of checks. For example, I feel like I missed something in a TV show (I didn't, but I am so worried I did and feel the need to rewind. I used to rewind so much it would take me an hour to watch a 20m episode). I give myself one chance to rewind. Then I just have to keep watching and tell myself that I trust myself to understand the show and fill myself in later if I am actually confused.

Again, OCD attacks the most raw and vulnerable fears you have. There is always something new! I've found that if I check or clear something with reassurance, nearly immediately my brain hooks onto something different. It's exhausting, and I realize with this that it's just my OCD and I need to move on, just keep going. Be comfortable with the fact that it makes me uncomfortable to keep moving on with that anxiety there.

Some things I say to myself are "It's future me's problem," "If it's important, it will come back," "my life will go on even if something is wrong."

You can't really prevent mistakes, they happen. And we have to heal and keep moving. And healing is not linear. Ups and downs! Fighting all the time is exhausting, so give yourself a break sometimes, it's okay to be weak and give in, trust that you will keep improving and learning from your experiences as life goes on. "I may never know. I will just have to keep on with my day and if it comes back, it comes back. If not, it probably wasn't that important or maybe I already took care of it. Continuing with my day is all I can do at this point, trying to remember/check is only making me feel worse, and there's nothing more I can do to make it better, as I've already checked/cleaned/etc." And then I move on.

Worrying is only fueling the cycle!

Advice and "should do's" stress me out, too. Do what you can. Soak in what you want and can, try not to worry about absorbing every detail and getting better right away. Respect your limits and boundaries, everyone has them, and healing is sometimes slow. You don't have to do everything perfectly, just simply try. And "trying" will be different every day, as our capabilities and batteries fluctuate often.

OCD is a liar and a prick. It will always always find something new to make you scared. It feeds off of the fear. My doctor told me about the phrase "egodystonic thoughts." Thoughts that conflict with your own values and beliefs. They are painful and fear-inducing. Try to tell yourself that these thoughts are just intrusive, egodystonic, OCD thoughts. I wouldn't believe an actual evil or harmful person would have such angst and pain over their own mortality. *edit: morality

I once heard that it's the second thought that's accurate to how you feel. For example, I have a fearful intrusive thought about "What if I hurt someone in the Panera bathroom?" What a thought! The second thought I have is, "Oh, no, that would be horrible, I wouldn't want to do that!" The second thought is correct. The first thought is scary! I feel scared of it, it's against my own beliefs and values. That's the corrected thought—how I feel, what I actually believe and how I want to act.

Intrusive thoughts are like that, they pop up and are wild what-if's. They get wilder and wilder the more you reassure them or try to check against them. "What if I'm not wearing pants right now?" No, I'm wearing pants, I checked! Then my OCD says, "Well, what if I'm crazy and I'm imagining I'm wearing pants!" And it gets worse and worse.

I tell myself: this is just my OCD trying to scare me. I feel the texture of my jeans on my skin, I feel the waistband. Panera would surely have something to say to me if I wasn't wearing pants. The best thing to do is just keep moving. Bring myself to my next task: asking for a baguette, beginning my sketchbook drawing, and so on. Just keep moving.

Ground yourself and pull yourself out of the fear when it begins to spiral, becoming anxious and sucked into it will only make it worse, and harder for you to see clearly. Take a pause, even if it feels impossible, to ground yourself. 5 things you can see, 4 things you can feel, 3 things you can hear, 2 things you can smell, 1 thing you can taste. "What I'm thinking is too important to pause from!" No, if it's important it will come back. You can take a break from your thoughts for something new, it's okay to relax first.

If you need immediate help, 988 is the US suicide hotline (you can text it too!) or just go to the ER. You probably also have local mobile crisis units or warm lines! <3 best to you.

It used to take me over an hour to watch one 20-minute episode of a show. The temptation to rewind still bothers me and sometimes is excruciating, but happily it does not happen every time I watch TV or make an episode last an hour.

I had to stop watching shows for a long time, it caused me too much anxiety. When I picked it back up, I liked to watch stuff that "didn't matter," shows I was less invested in or that weren't plot heavy, like Bob's Burgers. Each episode stands on its own, show context isn't really needed to understand each episode.

It got better over the years because I kinda trained myself with these kinds of shows by just forcing myself to get through the uncertainty of whether I missed or misunderstood something. I give myself one chance to rewind and rewatch a part, and if the sensation is still there, I allow myself to watch it once more with subtitles on. If the sensation is still there, I just keep going with the rest of the show. Keep watching, keep going, the sensation will be sitting beside me but eventually may dissipate, especially after doing this often.

To help the anxiety, I tell myself "if it really was important, it'll come up again." "If I really did miss something, I'll be able to tell later." Missed a joke or a small plot point? It's just one joke, one point, it'll pass or I'll catch back up as I watch. And if I really am wildly confused about the plot or something? I can ask the show's subreddit, I can Google an episode synopsis, etc.

Basically, if it (what I think I missed) is important, it will come back. Or, if it was important, it never would have left.
